extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Platonic philosophy / general readers interested in rhetoric and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and characterizes the dialogue's substantive claims about the nature, scope, ethical status, and effects of rhetoric as discussed by Socrates, Gorgias, and interlocutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as the art of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric 'is the artificer of persuasion, having this and no other business,' and 'persuasion is the chief end of rhetoric.' (Gorgias/Socratic formulation: rhetoric concerns discourse aimed at persuading judges, senators, citizens in courts and assemblies.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gorgias defines rhetoric as speech/discourse whose purpose is to persuade audiences in public assemblies and courts. Example contexts named: courts of law, council, assembly, political meetings. This serves as an evaluative definition: rhetoric is judged by its capacity to produce persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric produces belief without imparting knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric creates 'persuasion which gives belief without knowledge' rather than instruction about just and unjust; it persuades the many but does not teach them the truth (Socrates' critique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate rhetoric negatively where the standard is epistemic: if a mode of speech only produces belief and not knowledge, it is deficient as instruction. Socrates emphasizes that mass persuasion in short speeches cannot convey genuine understanding of complex moral/political matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric works through words and is a verbal art
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric is one of those arts which 'works and takes effect only through the medium of discourse'—like arithmetic, calculation, geometry—i.e., its instrument is speech rather than manual action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This locates rhetoric among arts whose primary means are verbal. The passage suggests evaluating arts by their operative medium (words vs physical action) and examining whether that medium suffices for the ends claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many arts are artificers of persuasion about their own subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Other arts (arithmetic, medicine, gymnastic, etc.) also 'persuade' people about their subject-matters: e.g., arithmetic persuades about odd and even numbers; medicine about diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an analytic criterion: rhetoric is not unique in producing persuasion. When assessing rhetoric's distinctiveness or legitimacy, compare it to other arts' pedagogical/persuasive functions and the truth-status of their claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as counterfeit/flattery of political art
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates characterizes rhetoric as part of a larger practice of 'flattery'—'the ghost or counterfeit of a part of politics'—a sham that imitates true political art but seeks pleasure and appearance rather than genuine good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard: if rhetoric merely imitates political knowledge (legislation/justice) without being concerned for citizens' true good, it is morally and intellectually inferior. Examples and anti-patterns: rhetoric that aims at gratification, popularity, or power rather than the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility for misuse versus teacher's blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Gorgias argues that if a pupil abuses rhetoric (like a boxer abusing his skill), the blame should fall on the wrong-doer, not the teacher; the teacher should not be held in detestation or banished for a pupil's perversion of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies a criterion for assigning moral responsibility: evaluate whether the originator/instructor of a skill is culpable for a pupil's immoral uses, or whether misuse is attributable to the agent who chooses to apply the skill wrongly. Socrates later challenges this when rhetoric's nature is questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between knowledge and belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates insists on a strict difference: 'having learned' (knowledge) is not the same as 'having believed'; there can be false belief but not false knowledge—knowledge and belief differ epistemically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rhetorical claims or outcomes, apply this epistemic criterion: does rhetoric produce knowledge (justified true belief) or merely belief (which may be false)? The distinction underpins much of the moral critique of rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral consequence: a just person must know justice and will not do injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument: one who has learned what is just is just; a just person will desire and do what is just and therefore will never willingly do injustice—so a genuine teacher of justice (including rhetoricians who teach about justice) must make just people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative criterion for evaluating the moral integrity of rhetoric: if rhetoric properly teaches justice, its students should be just; if rhetoric produces people willing to do injustice, it fails morally. Socrates uses this to press Gorgias on whether rhetoricians truly teach justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric's power can make the ignorant more persuasive than the knowledgeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates points out the danger that a rhetorician, though ignorant of a subject, can persuade the ignorant masses more effectively than the expert who actually knows, thereby enabling ignorance to triumph in public decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative test: assess rhetoric by its societal effects—does it amplify ignorance and lead to poor collective choices? Examples: elections, assemblies, choosing a physician or engineer where persuasion overrides expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as an experience producing gratification rather than a true art
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates (through the comparison to cookery) describes rhetoric as an 'experience' in producing 'delight and gratification'—part of flattery—not a genuine art aimed at the highest good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for classification: distinguish 'art' (techne) with objective goods and standards from techniques aimed at pleasure; rhetoric evaluated as mere gratification fails the standard of true arts that pursue real goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of arts: body vs soul; legislative/justice analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates maps arts onto body and soul: gymnastic/medicine for the body; legislation/justice for the soul; rhetoric is described as a sham that simulates the political (legislative/justice) arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a structural criterion for assessing whether rhetoric legitimately belongs to political arts: does it contribute to the health of the soul (true political good), or only simulate such contribution? Use the body/soul analogy to test adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric's claimed end: producing freedom and power over others
rubrics_metrics.description: Gorgias claims rhetoric's highest good is 'that which gives to men freedom in their own persons, and to individuals the power of ruling over others'—the ability to persuade judges, senators, and citizens to one's will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames a consequentialist criterion: evaluate rhetoric by whether its end is empowerment/power over others. The passage invites scrutiny of whether such power constitutes a true good or a corrupting aim (ties into the flattery critique).
